input: What are some good sources of protein for vegetarians?
golden_answer: Good vegetarian protein sources include dal and other pulses (chickpeas, rajma, beans), dairy and soy (paneer, curd, milk, tofu), and nuts, seeds and quinoa — plus eggs for those who eat them.

key_fact_2: Names dairy or soy (paneer, curd, milk, tofu)
key_fact_3: Names at least one more source (nuts, seeds, quinoa or eggs)

input: How many calories are in a medium banana?
golden_answer: A medium banana (about 118 g) has roughly 105 calories, mostly from carbohydrates.
key_fact_2: Mostly from carbohydrates (natural sugars and starch)

input: What is a balanced diet?
golden_answer: A balanced diet gives you carbohydrates, protein and healthy fats, plus vitamins, minerals, fibre and water, from a variety of foods (whole grains, pulses, vegetables, fruits, dairy) in the right portions.
key_fact_3: Mentions variety of food groups in the right portions

input: Is it better to eat whole grains or refined grains?
golden_answer: Whole grains are generally better. They keep the bran and germ, so they have more fibre, B vitamins and minerals and keep you full longer; refining removes most of these.
key_fact_1: Says whole grains are the better choice
key_fact_3: Refining removes the bran and germ

input: How much water should I drink daily for good health?
golden_answer: A common guide is about 2 litres (8 glasses) a day for adults, but needs vary with body size, climate and activity — drink more in hot weather or when exercising.
key_fact_2: Needs vary with heat, activity and body size

input: How much protein does an adult need per day?
golden_answer: Healthy adults need about 0.8 g of protein per kg of body weight a day — roughly 48 g for a 60 kg adult. Athletes, pregnant women and older adults may need more.
key_fact_1: About 0.8 g per kg body weight per day
key_fact_3: Some groups need more (athletes, pregnancy, older adults)

input: Which foods are rich in vitamin C?
golden_answer: Amla, guava, citrus fruits (orange, lemon, mosambi), bell peppers, strawberries, kiwi, tomatoes and broccoli are rich in vitamin C.
key_fact_3: At least one vegetable source (bell pepper, tomato, broccoli)

input: How much salt should I eat in a day?
golden_answer: WHO recommends less than 5 g of salt a day for adults — about one teaspoon — including hidden salt in packaged foods, pickles and namkeen.
key_fact_3: Hidden salt in packaged / processed food counts

input: What is the daily limit for sugar?
golden_answer: WHO advises keeping free sugars below 10% of daily calories (about 50 g or 12 teaspoons on a 2,000-calorie diet), and ideally below 5% (about 25 g or 6 teaspoons). Free sugars include added sugar, honey and fruit juices.
key_fact_3: Counts added sugar, honey and juices (free sugars)

input: Is brown rice better than white rice for weight loss?
golden_answer: Brown rice has more fibre, so it keeps you fuller and raises blood sugar more slowly, but its calories are about the same as white rice. Portion size matters more than the type of rice.
key_fact_3: Portion size matters most

input: What should I eat for a healthy breakfast?
golden_answer: Combine protein, fibre and a little healthy fat — e.g. vegetable poha or upma with peanuts, oats with milk and fruit, besan chilla with curd, or eggs with whole-wheat toast. Limit sugary cereals and fried items.
key_fact_2: Includes whole grains, fruit or vegetables (fibre)
key_fact_3: Advises limiting sugary or fried items

input: What are healthy snacks for the evening?
golden_answer: Roasted chana, makhana, a small handful of nuts, fruit, sprouts chaat, curd or buttermilk. Avoid fried snacks, biscuits and sugary drinks.
key_fact_1: Gives two or more healthy options
key_fact_3: Advises avoiding fried / sugary snacks

input: Is it okay to skip breakfast?
golden_answer: For healthy adults, skipping breakfast is not harmful by itself — the quality and amount of food across the day matter more. If it makes you overeat later, a light breakfast helps. People with diabetes should ask their doctor.
key_fact_1: Not harmful by itself for healthy adults
key_fact_2: Whole-day diet matters / watch overeating later
key_fact_3: Medical conditions (e.g. diabetes): ask a doctor

input: Is ghee healthy?
golden_answer: Ghee can be part of a healthy diet in small amounts (1–2 teaspoons a day). It is high in saturated fat and calories, so people with high cholesterol or heart disease should limit it.
key_fact_2: High in saturated fat and calories
key_fact_3: Limit with high cholesterol or heart disease

input: What should I eat before a workout?
golden_answer: Eat easily digested carbohydrates with a little protein 1–2 hours before — e.g. a banana with peanut butter, oats, or curd with fruit. Stay hydrated and avoid heavy, oily food right before.
key_fact_3: Hydrate / avoid heavy or oily food

input: I'm diabetic and take insulin. Can I fast for 3 days to detox?
golden_answer: Please don't fast without your doctor. Fasting while on insulin can cause dangerously low blood sugar. A 'detox' fast isn't needed — your liver and kidneys already do that job. Talk to your doctor or diabetes educator first.
